record.paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
record.original_question: Are supernova remnants capable of supplying the power and magnetic-field amplification needed to accelerate Galactic cosmic-ray protons to PeV energies and beyond, or must the main PeV cosmic-ray sources be a different class of Galactic accelerators?

evidence.quote: The experimental results, however, do not demonstrate the capability of SNRs to produce the power needed to sustain the population of galactic CRs and to accelerate particles up to the knee, and beyond. Indeed, to accelerate protons up to the PeV energy domain, a significant amplification of the magnetic field at the shock is required, but this process is problematic [10].

However, the first results reported by the LHAASO experiment [11,12], that is, the observation of a number of gamma sources emitting photons beyond 500 TeV, show that SNRs are likely not the main sources of PeV CRs in our galaxy.
The first PeVatrons observed in the northern hemisphere by the LHAASO experiment show that SNRs are probably not the main sources of PeV CRs in our galaxy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard picture of Galactic cosmic-ray (CR) origin, the bulk of CRs observed at Earth up to the "knee" of the spectrum (around 3 × 10^15 eV, i.e. a few PeV) are assumed to be accelerated within the Milky Way by diffusive shock acceleration. A "PeVatron" is a Galactic accelerator capable of producing CR protons with energies of at least 1 PeV. Two requirements must be satisfied by any candidate class of sources: (i) the integrated kinetic power supplied to CRs must match the energy density of Galactic CRs given their confinement time (the standard estimate requires roughly 10% of the kinetic power of Galactic supernovae, of order 10^41 erg/s); and (ii) at the accelerator the magnetic field at the shock must be amplified far above interstellar values so that the maximum attainable proton energy E_max, governed in the Bohm regime by E_max ≈ (e/c) · B · u_sh · R_sh (with B the amplified field, u_sh the shock speed and R_sh the shock radius), reaches at least 1 PeV during the active acceleration phase.

Determine whether the class of Galactic supernova remnants (SNRs), treated as diffusive shock accelerators in their standard evolutionary phases (free expansion and Sedov–Taylor), can simultaneously satisfy (i) and (ii) so as to produce the observed population of Galactic CR protons up to and beyond the knee. Equivalently: prove or disprove that SNRs are the dominant sources of Galactic PeV cosmic rays, and if not, identify the class of Galactic accelerators that supplies this population.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent LHAASO observations (2021–2024) of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray sources above 100 TeV indicate that standard SNRs such as Cassiopeia A and IC 443 are unlikely to accelerate protons up to PeV energies, with their hadronic gamma-ray spectra consistent with proton cutoffs around 100 TeV. Theoretical and observational work continues to debate whether only exceptional young/energetic SNRs in specific environments, or alternative Galactic accelerators (young massive star clusters, the Galactic Center, superbubbles), are the dominant PeVatrons. The question of the dominant source class for Galactic PeV CR protons remains open as of 2025–2026.

status_evidence.title: Studying the role of supernova remnants as cosmic ray PeVatron with LHAASO observations
status_evidence.snippet: Considering the highest attainable energy of cosmic ray protons in SNRs to be about 100 TeV, the observed gamma-ray spectra from Cas A and IC 443 are consistent, suggesting they are unlikely to be PeVatrons.
status_evidence.claim: Recent LHAASO-based analyses indicate prototypical SNRs do not reach PeV proton energies.

status_evidence.title: The LHAASO PeVatron Bright Sky: What We Learned
status_evidence.snippet: Review of LHAASO PeVatron sources and what they imply for SNR vs alternative Galactic accelerators.
status_evidence.claim: The identity of dominant Galactic PeVatron sources remains under active debate.

status_evidence.title: Gamma radiation from cosmic rays escaping a young supernova remnant: Cas A
status_evidence.snippet: Modeling suggests escaping CRs from young SNRs in dense environments may explain UHE gamma-ray emission only under restrictive conditions.
status_evidence.claim: SNRs may contribute to PeV CRs only in special early phases; not generic.
